title: The Akal Takht today
hook: the rebuilt Takht faces the Harmandir across the causeway

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Harmandir's day: prakash at dawn, hymns all day, and the Granth carried to rest at night. Your line was carried to rest.

Stand on the marble at the edge of the pool in Amritsar and turn slowly. In front of you, out on the water at the end of the causeway, the Harmandir Sahib, low and gold, full of singing. Behind you, on dry land, a tall white building with a gold dome. You can't look at both at once. You have to turn. Last night's palki crossed between them. Today, the second building as it stands now, and the line that runs between the two.
screen: `TURN SLOWLY ON THE MARBLE.` → `ONE ON THE WATER, ONE ON LAND.` → `YOU HAVE TO TURN.`

segments.voice: First, the building. The Akal Takht you see today has been rebuilt. This path told that story on an earlier day: after it was wrecked, Sikhs insisted on raising it again by their own hands, as kar seva. So it's new stone on old ground, and the place, Sikhs say, is what carries the authority. Second, the line. Tradition says Guru Hargobind raised his seat facing the Harmandir. Walk the causeway back, through the gateway at its end, and the Takht stands just beyond. One stands in the water, the other is raised on land. Third, what each one does. In the Harmandir, the Guru's hymns are sung from before dawn into the night. From the Akal Takht, the panth's decisions are made and its letters go out, as you heard on an earlier day. One is for listening, one is for answering, and neither has its back to the other. Fourth, the name over the second door. The opening lines of the Guru Granth Sahib describe God as akaal moorat, in paraphrase: a form beyond time. Akal, the Timeless. So the building that deals with worldly things, quarrels and rulings and the panth's business, carries the name of what is beyond time. Every night the Granth makes the crossing between them, the word carried across to where the decisions are made.
screen: `NEW STONE ON OLD GROUND.` · `ONE ON THE WATER, ONE RAISED ON LAND.` · `ONE FOR LISTENING, ONE FOR ANSWERING.` · `AKAL: THE TIMELESS.` · then, large: `FACING EACH OTHER.`

segments.voice: See the Harmandir in front of you, low and gold on the water, and breathe in, listening for the singing. Turn slowly to the Akal Takht behind you, raised and white, and breathe out with one decision that's waiting for you this week. Turn back and forth a few times, and let the two face each other inside you.
The Akal Takht today. The rebuilt throne of the Timeless at Amritsar, raised on land and facing the Harmandir across the courtyard. Today's word.
Your line: facing each other. Listening and answering, side by side, across one courtyard. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Pilgrims at Amritsar visit both the Harmandir Sahib and the Akal Takht, which face each other across the courtyard; the Guru Granth Sahib rests at the Akal Takht complex at night and returns to the Harmandir at dawn.

chat.says: Why does the Akal Takht face the Harmandir Sahib across the courtyard?
options: Hymns are sung in one, the panth's decisions made in the other; neither turns its back.
So the guards at the Takht can watch over the gold temple all night.
The Takht was built first, and the Harmandir was set to face it later.
chat.meaning: In the Harmandir hymns are sung; from the Akal Takht the panth's decisions go out. One listens, one answers, facing each other.

panth.meaning: the Sikh community as a whole
